headline: AI-assisted DSL built for infrastructure in 10 days
summary: A developer built a Domain Specific Language (DSL) that compiles to Kubernetes, Docker Compose, Helm, Terraform, and GitHub Actions, leveraging AI assistance.
details: The developer created Infra Lang, a Domain Specific Language (DSL) designed to manage infrastructure configurations, aiming to consolidate multiple formats like Kubernetes manifests, Docker Compose, and GitHub Actions into a single source of truth.

This new DSL compiles into five distinct targets: Kubernetes Deployments and Services, Docker Compose services, Helm charts, Terraform HCL, and GitHub Actions workflows. This approach aims to eliminate configuration drift and streamline development processes.

Infra Lang incorporates compile-time linting with 10 security rules and 13 reliability rules, catching issues like hardcoded secrets or single-replica databases before deployment. It also features a hand-written LALR(1) grammar for immediate error detection.

The project was developed with significant AI assistance, with Claude acting as a coding partner for approximately 40 sessions over 10 days. The AI primarily assisted with implementation and test writing, while the developer retained control over architectural decisions.

The development process uncovered 27 real-world bugs, including issues with secret encoding, service port naming, and Windows path conversion, highlighting the importance of testing against actual deployment targets.

Mutation testing revealed that high line coverage (93%) did not guarantee test effectiveness, with some modules scoring as low as 34% in mutation tests. Targeted fixes improved critical modules to 82-100% mutation score.

Cross-platform development challenges were encountered, particularly with file encoding on Windows and Docker daemon detection on CI runners. Explicit UTF-8 encoding and checking Docker info exit codes were among the solutions.

Building the Language Server Protocol (LSP) for Infra Lang provided deep insights into developer experience, enabling features like cross-file renaming, semantic tokens, signature help, and workspace indexing across all .infra files.

headline_marked: Generalist AI robots learn tasks from [[short videos]] without specific training
headline: Generalist AI robots learn tasks from short videos without specific training
summary: Startup Generalist AI's robots can master tasks like stacking cups or unzipping purses after watching a brief instructional video, demonstrating impressive real-world adaptability.
details: Startup Generalist AI is developing robots that can learn new tasks by watching short videos, bypassing the need for extensive, task-specific training.
During a demonstration, robot arms successfully stacked cups, placed blocks into bowls, and even improvised when tools were removed, showcasing a human-like ability to adapt.
One robot demonstrated impressive problem-solving by using a dustpan as a brush when the actual brush was unavailable, and another adapted its grip to successfully retrieve money from a purse.
CEO Pete Florence compares this learning capability to early large language models like GPT-3, where a simple prompt could enable the model to perform a new task.
The company focuses on teaching robots about real-world physics, which may contribute to their ability to transfer learned skills across different scenarios.
Generalist AI's approach involves collecting large-scale physical interaction data using special gloves with cameras, which humans wear to perform various chores.
Unlike some competitors, Generalist AI has built its AI models entirely from scratch, rather than relying on existing open-source language models.
Experts like Danfei Xu from Georgia Tech praise Generalist AI's execution and scientific rigor, noting their progress towards deployable robotic solutions.
caption:
